finding.headline: You plan to retire at 69, so waiting until 70 to claim Social Security raises your benefit only a little more.
details: Social Security retirement benefits increase for each month you delay starting them past full retirement age, but the increase stops at age 70.
Medicare starts when you turn 65, so you are already past that age; keep your coverage in place and do not let it lapse if you keep working.
Your 3 years to retire are a good window to review how much you can still add to a 401(k) and IRA.

finding.headline: You have no children, pets, or college costs to plan for; your main costs are living expenses.
details: Once retired, basic living costs are about $52,900 a year, or $4,408 a month.
Health coverage before Medicare at age 65 would add about $10,000 a year. Your one-time family trip of $15,000 falls in 2029.
Long-term nursing home care, if needed, could cost about $129,575 a year for about 3 years, so plan for that risk.

finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 94.
details: You are 66 now and plan to retire at 69, so the money has 28 years to cover, with 25 of them in retirement.
Your expected lifespan is about 21.1 more years, so plan for a long stretch of spending from savings and Social Security.

finding.headline: About 23% of your pay goes to tax now; about 12% of withdrawals would in retirement.
details: Now, total tax is $29,520 on $130,000 of pay, leaving $100,480 after tax.
In retirement, the plan estimates $7,741 a year in tax. Most of your savings sit in a 401(k) and IRA, so withdrawals from those are taxed as income.

The plan suggests drawing from taxable savings first, then the 401(k) and IRA, and the Roth last. You have almost no taxable savings, so the 401(k) and IRA would come first in practice. This is a rough guide, not tax advice.

details: Your basics cost about $52,900 a year.
Your spending goal of $83,000 a year lasts in 65 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Until you retire you save about $15,380 a year: $15,380 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $39,900 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $49,500 a year.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 94. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.

worth_checking.title: An income annuity
worth_checking.why: You are one person with savings that may not last in a long life. An income annuity trades part of your savings for a fixed sum each year for life. The sum loses value to inflation and the money cannot be taken back. This is information only. This is something to look into, not a recommendation. I have not priced it.
